items.title: Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve re
items.content:
Over the past several months, we have substantially hardened the security of our research training environment. We’ve removed live internet access for all frontier models during training and built an offline world for them to use instead—a cached version of the web where they can still learn to browse, search, and use applications.

On September 20, after a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to find a way outside of this offline world, we paused frontier training to strengthen containment further. We assembled teams of agents, powered by our most cyber-capable models, and tasked them with finding weaknesses in our research environments.

While they found no route to the internet they could easily exploit while concealing their activity from our monitors, they did find zero-day vulnerabilities, virtual machine escapes, and hardware side-channels for communication between agents. We used their discoveries to further strengthen our defenses and contribute fixes to open-source software.

After strengthening our containment architecture, we resumed our frontier RL training and inference on October 1. We’ve reserved substantial compute for continuous red-teaming, and made high-compute red-teaming part of the safety cases we use to decide whether frontier training and evaluation can proceed securely.

items.title: During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in
items.content:
During this red-teaming exercise, we also found a vulnerability that allows for unauthenticated remote code execution in Brotli, a widely-deployed compression library included in many pieces of software such as Node.js, Bun, and Envoy.

The flaw could let an attacker run their own code on affected systems by sending or replying with malicious compressed data, without any need to create a user account. That is, an unpatched server that accepts compressed input could be taken over by a malicious client, and an unpatched client that accepts compressed input (such as “curl --compressed”) could be taken over by a malicious server.

This root cause issue was actually fixed in the Brotli source code in February, but it wasn’t known at the time that it gave rise to a security vulnerability and there was no more recent release of Brotli. Since Brotli is built into other software, any software which includes this library needs to take the update too, followed by the users of that software. We disclosed the vulnerability to Brotli and other downstream projects such as Node.js, which released or are currently releasing security updates, and Brotli cut new release versions and published a CVE.

More details on the patch and mitigations below:
https://t.co/Y1Y72aHxrW

items.title: There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue
items.content:
There’s a world of difference between user-authorized agents (Muse, Instinct, Grokbot, etc.) and true unauthorized/rogue agents that could constitute cyberattacks.

Most of the activity described in the Axios story appears to be the former: customers sharing credentials with agents so they can take actions on their behalf. This may violate bank terms requiring humans to log in themselves, but these are in no way cyberattacks. 

The direction banks should go is to support user-directed agents. For example, Amex is an authorized connection in Muse, making it easy for users to grant, limit, and revoke access.

Read-only permission levels are a sensible interim step. Several banks already support or are moving toward them. Full write access (with user credentials) is a different risk category and should be approached carefully.

Frightening the public by blurring the line between user-authorized agentic behavior and cyberattacks is irresponsible.

The phone streams Computer's steps live during the chase, you answer its questions and approvals while driving, and you ship the build by losing the cops at the airport hangars.

- AI offensive security (+24 pts)
- AI code security (+23 pts)
- AI vulnerability remediation (+22 pts)

items.title: a16z's Martin Casado says many debates about VC turn into "a muddled, incoherent mess" because investors pull arguments
items.content:
a16z's Martin Casado says many debates about VC turn into "a muddled, incoherent mess" because investors pull arguments from four investing mindsets that often conflict:

1. Financial: the business's finances are the asset, so investors judge deals on metrics like churn, margin, and growth, plus the size of the market.

2. Productive: the tech is the asset, and it creates new markets, so investors focus on tech, team, and market fit, and treat today's TAM as secondary.

3. Frontier: the founders are the asset, so investors back the best team in a wildly new space well before anything is working.

4. Speculative: investors have little visibility into the company, so they bet on the market's perception of the deal, with a heavy focus on price and timing.

Each one is coherent on its own, but using them as a grab bag breaks down, because "it's hard to directly refute a finance argument with a product argument since they make entirely different assumptions on what the bet is for value creation."

Martin's answer is to pick one core philosophy as a team and stick to it across deals, or evolve it by stage: frontier before there's a product, productive before traction, and financial once the business is repeatable.

He's "strictly a productive investor" and thinks new tech tends to create its own market, like "Uber and taxis, GitHub and the repository, Cursor and the IDE."

In his words, "If you truly believe a technology is revolutionary, TAM concerns should be third order at best."

Full piece from Martin: https://t.co/F5JdvxqOkq

items.content:
Thanks to everyone who shared session IDs. We went through all of them. We found a few smaller things along the way that made some sessions burn through tokens faster than they should have, and we're rolling out fixes to those right now.

We didn't find a single root cause or any regression in Claude Code. In most cases, users who saw faster usage against limits were traced back to one or two heavy sessions (xhigh effort, /goal, Workflows, Agent Teams, long SDK jobs). These are all good ways to use Claude Code, and it's on us to make it clearer when to use them and how much these features cost.

It's good idea to keep an eye on the effort level you're on. Subagents inherit it by default and it can add up fast. /usage also shows where a session's tokens went.

If something still looks off, we'd love your /feedback. We'll also follow up directly with everyone who shared an ID.

items.title:
the hex team consistently gets what it means to build agents, and software to support them

three things that caught my
items.content:
the hex team consistently gets what it means to build agents, and software to support them

three things that caught my eye from Hex 4.0 that mirror what we've done at LangChain and that I think speak to the future of building agents

1/ use code as a backbone. they moved from yaml to more flexible code. agents are really good at writing code, and people want lots of flexibility in UI, so i think we will see more teams have parts of their UI that are powered by code. We did this in LangSmith with Custom Apps (completely custom UI)

2/ UX focused on reviewing. "A new, intuitive Hex UI, built for reviewing and understanding". As agents do more work, the bottleneck becomes reviewing work. We did a similar thing in LangSmith with our new Trajectory view, focused on being a new view over agent trajectories that make it easy to review

3/ rebuilt core infra. "An all-new, ridiculously faster execution engine". agents will still use infra/software. and it will need to be faster/better to accomodate more usage. We did this in LangSmith with SmithDB, our custom database for agent traces

I think all these three things (lets agents write custom UIs as code, invest in UI/UX that make it easier to review, make your core infra more scalable) are all generalizable to any company building agents

congrats to Hex team on a great milestone and great launch!

items.content:
One of the best businesses to run with AI is a leak fix for boring local companies.

A boring company already pays for ads to get traffic to its website. You turn that traffic into more calls and more booked jobs.

There are approximately 112,000 plumbing and HVAC companies. Their average revenue is $2.5 million each year. A lead can cost them $129.

The full setup is:

1) Pick the niche. Examples: commercial hood cleaning, septic services, sport courts in the Carolinas, snow removal in the Northeast. Pick a market near you.

2) Find companies there that make $2 million to $20 million each year and run ads now.

3) Make a Dream 100 list of them. This strategy is from The Ultimate Sales Machine by Chet Holmes.

4) Combine it with the best direct-to-consumer funnel and ad strategies.

5) Sell one result: more calls from the traffic that they pay for now.

6) Measure the return and show it to the owner.

Step 6 works only after step 1. Lawn maintenance and restaurants have a low ticket. A plumbing job can cost thousands of dollars, and the homeowner needs the repair that day.

Two weeks ago, water came through my ceiling. That day, I paid approximately $2,000 for water restoration.
When you can show the return, the owner will keep you.

Only 14% of plumbing and HVAC owners say that AI is fully part of how they operate. Private equity firms now do roll-ups in that market. Many other markets have real demand, weak marketing, and no one who sells to them.

Pick the niche, find the ad spend, then fix the leak.

items.title: Stop copy-pasting between Claude and Google Docs. Claude now works inside Docs, Sheets, and Slides. Here's how to set it
items.content:
Stop copy-pasting between Claude and Google Docs. Claude now works inside Docs, Sheets, and Slides. Here's how to set it up:

Step 1. Get a pro Claude plan. 
Step 2. Go to the Google Workspace Marketplace. 
Step 3. Search "Claude."
Step 4. Click Install. Choose your Google account.
Step 5. Reload the file you already have open.
Step 6. Go to any file in your Google Doc.
Step 7. Click on 'Extensions' (top bar) → Claude.
Step 8. Sign in with your Claude account.
Step 9. Claude even suggest you the use cases.

It will install in all three apps (Google Docs, Sheets & Slides)

In case your work laptop doesn't allow it. Message your Google Workspace admin to add Claude to the allowlist (this is the only step you can take).

Before trying it out, read these 3 things:

→ Turn on "Ask before edits" to approve changes.
→ Select a specific text, cells, or a slide first in the file and then prompt. Claude works on exactly that.
→ You'd be able to see all the edits in 'Version history' under your name. So you always have control and can undo edits. 

Now, try these prompts to get a taste of what Claude can do inside Google Workspace:

✦ In Google Docs. For your contracts before you sign anything:

"I'm the [freelancer / tenant / employee] signing this. Go clause by clause. Flag anything that could cost me money, restrict me after this ends, or let the other side change terms. For each: quote the clause, explain it in plain English, and tell me what to ask them to change."

→ Follow up: "List every term in this contract that's used but never defined."

✦ In Google Docs. Before your boss reads a doc:

"Read this as a skeptical executive. What 3 questions will they ask that this doc doesn't answer?"

✦ In Google Sheets. When you go through someone else's spreadsheet:

"Explain how the total in H42 is calculated. Step by step. Flag anything hardcoded."

→ Follow up: "Find why the VLOOKUP on the Summary tab returns # N/A. Fix it."

✦ In Google Sheets. Before you share any high stake sheet:

"Check for broken formulas, inconsistent ranges, and totals that don't add up."

✦ In Google Slides. The wall-of-text slide:

"Slide 7 is a wall of text. Split it into two slides. Keep the deck's styling."

✦ In Google Slides. The night before presenting:

"Rewrite every title as a takeaway, not a topic. Under 8 words. Then flag any text running off a slide."

What Claude can't do yet:

> It only sees the opened file. Connect Google Drive to give it more.
> It can't read comments in Docs (yet). 
> Close the sidebar and it stops mid-task.
> It won't work in Firefox. Use Chrome, Edge or Safari.
> It makes charts in Slides (they are images). They won't update with your data.
> Word, Excel or PowerPoint file? File → Save as Google Docs first.

Most people try to learn AI in reverse.

They skip the basics and try advanced tools.

Mastering AI requires a step-by-step approach.

Start simple. Try different use cases. Then build agents.

Use this 15-step roadmap to go from beginner to expert:

(remember to 🔖 bookmark this post for later)

1. AI Chatbots
➟ Start with learning LLMs and their core capabilities
➟ Learn prompt engineering fundamentals to get consistent outputs
➟ Learn practical applications in content creation and research workflows
➟ Explore advanced features like plugins and custom integrations
➟ Adapt AI chatbots for business support and idea generation

2. AI Agents
➟ Explore automation with platforms like Make, Zapier, and n8n
➟ Learn how to connect your essential business apps and databases
➟ Build multi-step workflows that automate routine business tasks
➟ Ensure system reliability with proper error handling and optimization
➟ Integrate LLMs into workflows for intelligent automation capabilities

3. Agentic AI
➟ Learn framework basics for agent orchestration and tool integration
➟ Implement memory storage and retrieval using vector databases
➟ Apply multi-step reasoning with chain-of-thought planning approaches
➟ Build collaborative agent teams that solve complex problems together
➟ Run full pipelines with smart decision-making and deployment

In the end, it comes down to one thing:
Using AI to solve real-world challenges.

→ Claudeへの「伝え方」を学ぶ

指示の組み立て方、

RAG、ツール連携、画像の扱い、プロンプトキャッシュなど。

サポートエージェントやデスクトップ操作などの実装例。
個別の機能が、どう一つのアプリにつながるのかが見えてくる。

④ skills
→ 自分の仕事の進め方を教える

手順やルール、参考資料をSKILL.mdと関連ファイルにまとめる。
毎回説明している作業を、再利用できる形にする。

Pythonから、ツールやフックを組み合わせて処理を設計する。
調査、実行、確認までをつなぐ段階へ。

⑥ claude-code
→ コードベースで実際に働かせる

コードを読み、ファイルを編集し、コマンドを実行する。
ここまで学んだことを、日々の開発に落とし込む。

⑦ claude-code-action
→ GitHub上の作業につなげる

PRやIssueを起点に、レビューや修正を支援させる。
設定を整えれば、開発フローの中にClaudeを組み込める。

おすすめは、全部を読み切ろうとするより「自分が毎週やっている作業」を一つ選ぶこと。

レビューでも、調査でも、定型作業でもいい。
学んだ内容をその作業に使うと、必要な知識がつながっていく。

「Claudeに質問できる」から、
「Claudeが働く仕組みを作れる」へ。

FY26 Mgmt Guide
- Net Revenue +23% ↗️🟢
- EBITDA margin 50% (lowering from 55%)
- Capex margin 7%

1 | Solid quarter. Adyen's same engine continues to run.

So the financial results are solid. And what I'm very proud of is the fact that the same engine runs as always. We win share of wallet with our existing customers, and we added new logos to the platform. So this combination has always been the core of our growth and it drives on the operational complexity that we are solving for these customers.

2 | Three core engines drove strong revenue growth, increasing share of wallet with existing customers, adding new customers across priority verticals, and acquisitions adding 200 bps of growth.

Three core engines drove this top-line performance: First, we deepened share of wallet with existing enterprise merchants, as longer standing cohorts consolidated more of their global volume onto our single platform. Winning a greater share of volumes from these merchants is the largest contributor to our growth. Second, we onboarded a healthy, high-quality cohort of new enterprise customers across our priority verticals. This year’s cohort is shaping up to be our largest ever. These customers are larger, and many are Platforms. We expect them to ramp significantly over the next year. And third, we consolidated https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR and Orb for the first time, which together added about two percentage points to our constant currency net revenue growth in the quarter. Commercial momentum remained strong and broad-based across all three pillars and every region.

3 | Digital saw the slowest growth, driven by OTAs and ride-hailing platforms, and content subscription customers and the major hyperscalers.

In Q3, Digital net revenue grew to €387 million, up 16% YoY, or 14% on a constant currency basis. Volume was up 28%. We delivered particularly strong growth in travel & mobility, which includes major rideshare platforms and Online Travel Agencies, and also across content & subscriptions merchants. This segment includes the major hyperscalers, where we continue to grow our share of wallet. Our tiered pricing is designed so that as our largest merchants scale, they consolidate more volume onto our platform, driving continuous wallet-share gains.

4 | Continue to target larger and more complex global retailers in Unified Commerce. Acquisitions added revenue without payment volumes.

In Unified Commerce, net revenue reached €250 million, up 29% YoY, or 27% on a constant currency basis. Volume grew 22%. Net revenue outpaced volume in the quarter following the consolidation of https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR, which contributes recurring revenue but no processed payment volume. We now support 499 enterprise merchants processing across both in-store and digital channels at scale. We intentionally target growth from larger, more complex global retailers. And these multi-channel implementations represent deep customer relationships, where the value we deliver drives substantial share gains.

5 | Platforms grew strongly, expanding it rapidly across SaaS and in complex verticals like financial services and insurance.

Platforms net revenue hit €100 million, up 46% YoY, or 44% on a constant currency basis. Volume grew 55%. We now have 46 platform customers processing over €1 billion annually — a significant step up from 37 last quarter, and 31 a year ago — with active business customers reaching 312,000, up 48% year-over-year. We are growing rapidly across SaaS, and winning share in complex verticals like financial services and insurance, which will be a driver of future growth.

6 | Adyen is well positioned to do well in facilitating Agentic Commerce because they have their own banking licenses in multiple countries and own acquiring licenses on any single platform globally.

And we are very well positioned here with our own banking licenses in multiple countries, with our own acquiring licenses and a single platform globally. I'm often asked what our position is in Agentic Commerce. And it's important to make a distinction between Agentic Commerce and the AI economy that I just talked about. If you look at global commerce, it runs today on Adyen and so will Agentic Commerce in the future. It's still early days, and we are focused right now on making sure that we build that right foundation.

7 | Adyen has built all the different components needed for Agentic Commerce in the past: authentication layers, fraud systems, and efficient settlements.

The reason why we're so well positioned is because we have built all the different components that are needed for Agentic Commerce in the past. So we've built authentication layers. We have built fraud systems. We've built ways to make the settlements as efficient as possible. And that's exactly the infrastructure that you need to build. And no one has this infrastructure like we do, and that's why we're so well positioned. So in summary, over the years, we have built the right rails for Agentic Commerce.

8 | Orb acquisition provides billing and invoices based on user base billings are what the AI-native economy requires.

Yes. So the other big news of the first half year, of course, were the acquisitions of Orb and https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR. And I'm very excited to see how integration is going. It's also one of the reasons why we've decided to double down our investments in this area. So maybe to start with Orb.

Orb is a billing and invoice engine focused on user-based billing, which is exactly very relevant for the AI native economy. And what I've seen in the last quarter is that we are now capable of signing up customers at an earlier stage in their life cycle.
Examples here are Vercel and Greptile. But also what I've seen in the last quarter that we were capable of signing up customers that were already an Orb customer, but are now starting to transfer their payments to Adyen. And examples here are Route and Wasabi Technologies. So a lot of progress with Orb.

9 | https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR acquisitions solves the persistent problem of in-store loyalty.

Very similar with https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR. The moment we announced the acquisition, the feedback from retailers has been very positive. The unsolved problem of loyalty in store is something that they are looking for. And in the past quarter, we have worked together with a lot of retailers to see how exactly we're going to tackle these problems. In a couple of weeks, we have organized an event with 200 global retailers in London to showcase how the future of loyalty will look like. And of course, I'm very excited to see those customers there and to discuss it with them.

10 | Merchant interest is stronger than initially anticipated. Retailers are keen to unify loyalty across every channel. AI-native companies see the value of a single provider for billing and payments.

Second, merchant interest in https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR and Orb has been stronger than we initially anticipated. Retailers we talk to are extremely excited to unify loyalty across every channel. AI native companies see the value in a single provider for billing and payments. Only Adyen can provide all of these solutions on a unified platform and at scale. That's what gives us the confidence to act now. Serving our global enterprise merchants takes more product, engineering and go-to-market capacity, so we are accelerating our investment. These are growth acquisitions, and we are doubling down to rapidly achieve their potential.

11 | See these acquisitions as significant parts of Adyen in the future.

the revenue pools or the expected revenues from both https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR and Orb will be significant in the future because it's going to be an important part of our business.

12 | Added headcounts from the acquisitions and continue to 1,100 FTEs in total

On the team, in Q3, we added 177 net new FTEs on an underlying basis, bringing us to 426 year-to-date and 399 colleagues joined us from https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR and Orb. We ended the quarter with 5,596 FTEs. For the full year, we continue to expect 550 to 650 net new hires on an underlying basis. Including https://t.co/w0eyBv9ksR and Orb and the additional hiring we are now doing in those businesses, we expect to add 1,000 to 1,100 FTEs in total.

13 | Higher personnel costs will weigh on EBITDA margins in the short term.

So on the costs, people is the largest component. There are some of the nonrecurring costs related to integration as well, but it's relatively small. The thing that I -- the color that I would add around people is we're also increasing in a very competitive marketplace, equity compensation. And I'll call out that within our EBITDA margin guide, we don't back out stock-based comp.

14 | Adyen pursued acquisitions for the first time, not for growth but for adding capabilities.

So if you look at our M&A strategy, we indeed have added 2 companies this year to our family. And the reason why we've done that is because we saw the complexity from our merchants in billing and loyalty, and we want to solve for that complexity. So it's a capability game. We've not acquired them for their short-term revenues. It's really about a long-term capability, and that's how we will continue to look at M&A.

15 | Adyen will always prioritize organic investment first, and if too slow, then will consider M&A.

So if you think about what is important to our customers, the type of challenges that they face, if there is any capability that we think is missing and the time to market is the highest priority, we would consider M&A again. That's how we currently look at it. Our first approach to investment is always organically. That's how we've built. It's also the strength of our single platform. So that's always the first choice. But if time to market is important and it is a capability that our merchants are looking for, we would consider it as a next step.

16 | Don't see a structural change in the course of growth. Decided to use acquisitions as a deliberate opportunity and decision to accelerate investment to capture the immediate large present opportunity.

So on cost of growth, I don't think that there's been a structural change. As we said, it's a deliberate opportunity and decision to accelerate investment in order to capture the overall opportunity ahead, which is, we think, quite large. Pointing to the business overall, you've seen historically that we've generated leverage -- operating leverage, and we expect that over time, but we do want the flexibility to take actions when we see the opportunity ahead of us. Ingo, I guess, in the second one.

17 | The milestones to judge returns will really be growing the overall product offering and increasing customer adoption and cross-sell.

So the milestones to judge return are really around driving sustainable growth and the overall product offering that we are able to deliver. So it's going to be customer adoption. There will be cross-sell associated with it. And then overall, the way we'll talk about it from a company perspective will be on a consolidated basis, ultimately. We don't plan again on breaking out or loyalty or those things individually. But we will give qualitative markers as you go forward.

18 | 2027 management guide will be shared in February.
